bib.title: Adversarial NLI: A New Benchmark for Natural Language Understanding
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020), pages 4885-4901

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; Table 12 extra examples and UI figures (Figs 8-10) only skimmed.

question: Can a large NLI benchmark be built by iterative adversarial human-and-model-in-the-loop collection so that it is harder than existing sets, lasts longer, and also improves model training?
hypothesis: Human annotators, even non-experts, can find weaknesses of current SOTA models; training on the resulting examples improves robustness and the moving-target procedure resists saturation.
contributions: A human-and-model-in-the-loop NLI dataset of three rounds of increasing difficulty and complexity with annotator-provided explanations.
Training on it gives state-of-the-art results on a variety of popular NLI benchmarks.
Detailed analysis of the data: shortcomings of current models, inference-type categorisation, good performance on NLI stress tests.

method.summary: Annotators on Mechanical Turk write a hypothesis for a given context and target label (entailment/neutral/contradiction) to fool the current best model, which shows label probabilities as feedback. Model-wrong examples are verified by 2-3 other humans; verified ones form dev/test, all others go to train; a stronger model is trained on the augmented data for the next round (HAMLET). Three rounds (A1-A3) were collected; BERT/XLNet/RoBERTa are trained on mixes of SNLI, MNLI, FEVER-NLI and ANLI and evaluated.
method.task: natural language inference (3-way classification), dataset collection and evaluation

datasets.name: ANLI A1
datasets.source: Wikipedia contexts (250-600 chars) from HotpotQA training set, ground-truth or TF-IDF retrieved
datasets.preprocessing: dev/test only verified model-wrong examples; test restricted to exclusive annotators and label-balanced

datasets.name: ANLI A3
datasets.source: Wikipedia, news (Common Crawl), fiction (StoryCloze, CBT), spoken text (MASC court and debate transcripts), WikiHow, RTE5 long contexts

datasets.name: SNLI
datasets.size: inferred: part of 943k SNLI+MNLI training examples

datasets.name: FEVER NLI version
datasets.source: claims paired with evidence retrieved by Nie et al. (2019)

datasets.name: SNLI-Hard and NLI stress tests
datasets.split: models tuned on each test's own dev set
datasets.source: Gururangan et al. 2018; Naik et al. 2018

other.use: Round 1 adversary, trained on SNLI+MNLI, best model they could train

other.R2: trained on SNLI, MNLI, FEVER-NLI, A1; hyperparameter search selected on A1 dev, then several seeds; random ensemble member per annotator turn
other.R3: adds A2 to training data; ensemble

training.seeds: several random seeds for the R2/R3 ensembles, number not stated

other.hyperparameter_selection: best on A1 dev for R2 model

inference.samples: Single reported accuracy per row; number of seeds for reported rows not stated
inference.retrieval: TF-IDF (Chen et al. 2017) retrieval for some A1/A2 contexts

parameters.verification: 2 verifiers must agree with writer, a third breaks ties, else discarded
parameters.test_restriction: exclusive annotators never in training; label-balanced (and genre-balanced where applicable)

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of test examples labelled correctly

metrics.name: model error rate
metrics.definition: percentage of examples the model got wrong; verified = confirmed by at least 2 human annotators

metrics.name: tries
metrics.definition: attempts per context until a model error found

metrics.name: Fleiss kappa
metrics.definition: inter-annotator agreement for writers and first two verifiers

eval.protocol: Test accuracy per round, ANLI total, ANLI-E (exclusive annotators), SNLI test and MNLI dev; equal-size downsampling comparisons; no seeds or significance tests stated

evidence.where: Table 2 shows 16,946 train, 1,000 dev, 1,000 test; text says approximately 19k for Round 1

results.table: Table 3, row RoBERTa S,M,F,ANLI, column A3

results.quote:
The state of the art on
SNLI is currently held by MT-DNN (Liu et al.,

results.claim: MNLI dev matched 91.0 and mismatched 90.7 versus 90.2 in the RoBERTa paper.
results.setup: MNLI dev-m, RoBERTa fine-tuned with ANLI

results.claim: Hypothesis-only RoBERTa trained on ANLI only gets 51.0 / 42.6 / 41.5 on A1-A3 but 51.9 / 54.5 on MNLI.
Training on ANLI only (~163k examples) matches BERT trained on SNLI+MNLI (943k) at about 86 on MNLI.
Adversarial data is more data-efficient: with equal training size SMD1+A scores 72.6 on A1 versus 45.1 for SMD1+SMD2.
Verified examples are much more valuable than unverified ones; unverified drops to random in later rounds.
results.setup: RoBERTa, downsampled to equal size, Fig 3

results.claim: ANLI-trained RoBERTa (All) gets 85.9/82.1 on the Antonym stress test versus 14.4/10.2 for the previous model.
results.setup: NLI stress test AT matched, tuned on own dev

results.claim: Fleiss kappa for writers and first two verifiers is 0.7210 on A1 dev+test, 0.6910 on A2, 0.6786 on A3.
results.table: Table 10, row A3, column Dev + Test

results.claim: Numerical and quantitative reasoning share of tagged dev examples falls from 38% in A1 to 10% in A3.

results.table: Table 7, row A3, column Numerical & Quant.

limits: Training examples were not verified, so some noise remains in training data.
Compared with static collection, the paper gives no cost or time trade-off; leaves it to future work.
Unclear how to apply the method to generative tasks.
Some hypothesis bias remains (hypothesis-only is slightly above chance on ANLI).
Training hyperparameters, seeds and compute for all models are not stated.
Only three rounds; saturation by later models (not tested here) has since occurred; not assessed in text.
Round 3 mixes new domains with a stronger model, so round-to-round difficulty is partly confounded by context change.
